Let $a$ = first term and $r$ = common ratio

Then $ar^3=48$ ——— (1)

and $ar^7=\dfrac{3}{16}$ ——— (2)

Dividing (2) by (1),
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{ar^7}{ar^3}&=\dfrac{\frac{3}{16}}{48}\\\therefore\ r^4&=\dfrac{1}{256}\\\therefore\ r&=\pm\dfrac{1}{4}\end{aligned}$$
If $r=\dfrac{1}{4}$, $a\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)^3=48$ $\therefore\ a=3072$

If $r=-\dfrac{1}{4}$, $a\left(-\dfrac{1}{4}\right)^3=48$ $\therefore\ a=-3072$

solutions.latex:
Area of concrete path is $2y+x-2$
$$\begin{aligned}A&=2\left(\dfrac{50}{x-2}+1\right)+x-2\\A&=2\left(\dfrac{50}{x-2}\right)+2+x-2\\A&=\dfrac{100}{x-2}+x\\&=100(x-2)^{-1}+x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}A'&=100\left(-1(x-2)^{-2}\right)+1\\&=\dfrac{-100}{(x-2)^2}+1\end{aligned}$$
$A'=0$ when
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{-100}{(x-2)^2}&=-1\\100&=(x-2)^2\\\pm10&=x-2\\x&=12\text{ or }-8\end{aligned}$$
Since $x$ is a distance, discard $-8$.

Stationary point at $x=12$.
$$\begin{array}{c|ccc}x&11&12&13\\\hline A'&\dfrac{-100}{81}+1&0&\dfrac{-100}{121}+1\\&\searrow&-&\nearrow\end{array}$$
So there is a minimum turning point at $x=12$.

The minimum area of the path is when $x=12$.

$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=3x^2-6x-8$$
Tangent at $(-1,6)$ is $y=x+7$

Slope of tangent is 1.

Solve $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=1$ ie
$$\begin{aligned}3x^2-6x-8&=1\\3x^2-6x-9&=0\\3(x^2-2x-3)&=0\\3(x-3)(x+1)&=0\end{aligned}$$
So $x$ coordinate of $R$ is 3.

When $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=3x^2-6x-8$
$$y=x^3-3x^2-8x+k\quad\text{and when }x=-1\ \ y=6.$$
$$\begin{aligned}\text{So}\quad6&=(-1)^3-3(-1)^2-8(-1)+k\\6&=-1-3+8+k\\6-4&=k\\k&=2\end{aligned}$$
When $x=3$
$$\begin{aligned}y&=x^3-3x^2-8x+2\\&=27-27-24+2\\&=-22\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ Coordinates of $R$ are $(3,-22)$.

$$\begin{aligned}f'(x)&=e^{-x}\cos x+-e^{-x}\sin x\\&=e^{-x}(\cos x-\sin x)\end{aligned}$$

$$x=\dfrac{\pi}{4}\text{ or }\dfrac{5\pi}{4}$$

The two stationary points are
$$\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4},\dfrac{e^{-\frac{\pi}{4}}}{\sqrt{2}}\right)\quad\text{and}\quad\left(\dfrac{5\pi}{4},\dfrac{-e^{-\frac{5\pi}{4}}}{\sqrt{2}}\right)$$
approx.

solutions.latex:
We want the equation $e^{-2x}=e^{-x}+k$ to have 2 solutions.

ie $e^{-2x}-e^{-x}-k=0$ has 2 solutions

ie $\left(e^{-x}\right)^2-\left(e^{-x}\right)-k=0$ has 2 solutions

Using the quadratic formula,
$$e^{-x}=\dfrac{1\pm\sqrt{1+4k}}{2}$$
For two real solutions we want $1+4k>0$, ie $k>-\dfrac{1}{4}$

But for two solutions for $e^{-x}$, both the real solutions to the quadratic must be positive.
$$\begin{aligned}\therefore\ \sqrt{1+4k}&<1\\\therefore\ 1+4k&<1\\\therefore\ k&<0\end{aligned}$$
Hence $-\dfrac{1}{4}<k<0$.
